_meta.title: ToxiScan ingredient database - verified corrections
_meta.language: All descriptions are written in English (field: description_en). This is the source language.
instructions_for_rork: 1. Apply each entry according to its _action field: REPLACE (overwrite the existing entry matching 'name'), ADD (create a new entry), DELETE (remove the entry), SPLIT (create as a new separate entry, and apply the companion REPLACE that strips its aliases from the parent).
2. Translate every description_en into French (description_fr) and Korean (description_ko). Keep the English as the source of truth: if a translation and the English ever diverge, the English wins.

3. Translation rules: keep regulatory bodies untranslated as acronyms (EFSA, IARC, FDA, WHO/OMS, EU/UE). Keep E-numbers exactly as written (E250, not E-250). Keep IARC group names in the standard French form: Group 1 = Groupe 1, Group 2A = Groupe 2A, Group 2B = Groupe 2B. Do not soften or dramatise: translate the claim exactly as calibrated in English.
4. Do NOT let the AI rewrite or embellish these descriptions at scan time. They are fixed, sourced text, per the product decision already made.
5. After import, delete these 4 entries which are now duplicates because their aliases were merged elsewhere: 'sirop d'erable deshydrate', 'sucre de coco', 'sucre de datte', 'melasse de malt'.

6. The _reason, _source, _priority and _batch fields are internal documentation. Strip them before writing to the app database, but keep them in your repository so any claim can be traced back to its source if a user challenges it.
_meta.verification_note: Every regulatory and IARC claim in this file was checked against the primary source cited in _source. Where sources conflicted or evidence was weak, the claim was removed rather than asserted - see entries 'phosphate d'os', 'reishi' and 'gelee royale'.

corrections._reason: IARC Group 1 applies to processed meat as a food, not to the nitrate additive. IARC classifies ingested nitrate under nitrosation conditions as Group 2A.
corrections._source: IARC Monographs vol. 94 (2010)
corrections.name: nitrate de sodium
corrections.description_en: A curing salt (E251) that the body converts to nitrite, which can then form nitrosamines. IARC rates ingested nitrate under conditions leading to endogenous nitrosation as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic. The confirmed Group 1 classification applies to processed meat as a food, not to the additive on its own.

corrections._reason: E1450 is NOT hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate (that is E1442). E1450 is starch sodium octenyl succinate.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: amidon octenylsuccinate de sodium
corrections.description_en: Starch modified with octenyl succinic anhydride (E1450) to act as an emulsifier and encapsulating agent in drinks, dressings and powdered flavourings. EFSA's 2017 re-evaluation of modified starches found no safety concern and no need for a numerical ADI, but it remains a refined carbohydrate with no nutrients and a marker of industrial formulation.

corrections._reason: Recovers the aliases wrongly attached to E1450.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: phosphate de diamidon hydroxypropyle
corrections.description_en: One of the most common modified starches (E1442), used in sauces, desserts and ready meals to hold texture through heating and freezing. EFSA's 2017 re-evaluation found no safety concern and set no numerical ADI, but it is a purely technical refined carbohydrate and a clear marker of ultra-processed food.

corrections._reason: EFSA assessed all 12 modified starches in a single opinion with one conclusion. E1404 was alone in Occasional while its siblings were Processed.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: oxidized starch
corrections.description_en: Starch chemically oxidised (E1404) to improve thickening, clarity and processing performance. EFSA's 2017 re-evaluation of the whole modified-starch family found no safety concern and no genotoxic concern. Its role is purely technological: a refined carbohydrate that signals an industrially engineered texture.

corrections._reason: Same modified-starch family alignment.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: phosphated distarch phosphate
corrections.description_en: A cross-linked and phosphorylated starch (E1413) designed to resist heat, acid and mechanical processing. EFSA found no safety concern for the modified-starch family, but the additive brings no nutrition and marks a heavily formulated product.

corrections._reason: Same modified-starch family alignment.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: amidon hydroxypropyl
corrections.description_en: A chemically modified starch (E1440) that stays stable through freezing, heating and storage. EFSA's 2017 opinion raised no safety or genotoxicity concern, but it is a refined carbohydrate whose only purpose is texture in industrial recipes.

corrections._reason: Same modified-starch family alignment.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: acetylated oxidized starch
corrections.description_en: A starch both oxidised and acetylated (E1451) to improve stability, clarity and texture. EFSA found no safety concern for the modified-starch family, but the double chemical treatment leaves a refined carbohydrate used purely as a structural ingredient.

corrections._reason: The description cited '(E1404)' although this entry is the generic labelling term, not a specific E number.
corrections._source: Regulation (EC) 1333/2008 ; EFSA Journal 2017;15(10):4911
corrections.name: amidon modifie
corrections.description_en: A generic label covering any starch altered chemically or physically to thicken and stabilise industrial food, without saying which one. EFSA considers modified starches safe with no numerical ADI needed, but they are refined carbohydrates with no nutrients and one of the clearest markers of ultra-processing.

corrections._reason: Badge disproportionate: the EU delisting was caused by MISSING data, not by demonstrated toxicity. The description contradicted its own badge.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 2018/98 ; EFSA Journal 2015;13(6):4144
corrections.name: calcium sorbate
corrections.description_en: A preservative deleted from the EU list of authorised food additives in 2018 because no company ever supplied the genotoxicity data EFSA had asked for - a data gap, not a proven toxicity. EFSA had already excluded it from the group ADI shared by sorbic acid (E200) and potassium sorbate (E202), partly because the related sodium salt tested positive for genotoxicity. It is no longer permitted in EU food.

corrections._reason: E903 was Processed while E901 and E902 were Approved, for an identical EFSA conclusion.
corrections.name: cire de carnauba
corrections.description_en: A plant wax from the leaves of the Brazilian carnauba palm, used to glaze sweets, chewing gum, coffee beans and coated tablets. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2012 and found no genotoxicity concern and sufficient margins of safety at authorised uses. It is practically not absorbed by the gut - the same conclusion reached for candelilla wax (E902).

corrections._reason: Same substance as 'alpha-tocopherol' (Approved) but badged Occasional.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2015;13(9):4247
corrections.name: d-alpha tocopherol
corrections.description_en: The natural RRR form of vitamin E, the one with the highest vitamin activity in the body. It protects cells and dietary fats from oxidation. EFSA re-evaluated the tocopherol family (E306-E309) in 2015 and found no safety concern at the levels used in food.

corrections._reason: The description said EFSA could not conclude for lack of nanoparticle data - that is the silver (E174) text, not gold. EFSA 2016 concluded systemic effects are not expected.
corrections._source: EFSA ANS Panel, E175 opinion (January 2016)
corrections.name: or
corrections.description_en: Gold leaf (E175) used to decorate confectionery and drinks. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2016 and concluded that, given the very low solubility of elemental gold, systemic absorption and systemic effects are not expected. It passes through the body unchanged and adds nothing nutritionally - purely decorative.

corrections._reason: EFSA published a follow-up in April 2025 confirming it still cannot conclude on safety.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2025;23(4):9316
corrections.name: argent
corrections.description_en: Silver (E174), used as a decorative coating on confectionery. EFSA could not conclude on its safety in 2016, and its 2025 follow-up confirmed that the data on nanoparticle content, silver-ion release and genotoxicity are still inadequate. Nearly a decade on, its safety as a food additive remains officially unresolved.

corrections._reason: The 'detected in breast tumours' claim came from Darbre 2004, which established no causal link and has been widely contested. Replaced with the regulatory record, which is verifiable and stronger.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 358/2014 ; Commission Regulation (EU) 1004/2014 ; SCCS opinions 2013 and 2021
corrections.name: parabene
corrections.description_en: A family of preservatives with weak hormone-like activity in laboratory tests. The EU banned five of them from cosmetics in 2014 for lack of safety data (isopropyl-, isobutyl-, phenyl-, benzyl- and pentylparaben) and capped propyl- and butylparaben at 0.14%, with an additional ban on the nappy area of children under three. The 2004 study that detected parabens in breast tissue established no causal link; the real issue is cumulative exposure across food, cosmetics and medicines.

corrections._reason: The description listed only benefits while the badge was Occasional - the user could not understand the yellow.
corrections._source: IARC Monographs vol. 114 (2015)
corrections.name: viande rouge
corrections.description_en: Rich in bioavailable iron, zinc and vitamin B12, which support blood and immune function. IARC classified red meat as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans, in 2015, based mainly on colorectal cancer - which is why it belongs in a balanced diet as a regular but moderate item rather than a daily one.

corrections._reason: Processed badge KEPT against the other polyols in Occasional, but the description did not explain why.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2023;21(12):8430 ; Witkowski et al., Nature Medicine 2023;29:710-718
corrections.name: erythritol
corrections.description_en: A polyol sweetener produced by fermentation. EFSA re-evaluated it in 2023 and, for the first time ever, set an ADI based on an immediate effect - diarrhoea - at 0.5 g/kg body weight per day, then concluded that both acute and chronic intake exceed that ADI in every age group. Separate Cleveland Clinic work links circulating erythritol to platelet reactivity and cardiovascular events; that is association plus mechanism rather than proof, but it is enough to set it apart from older polyols.

corrections._reason: Same justification as erythritol: what distinguishes it from the polyols left in Occasional.
corrections._source: Witkowski et al., European Heart Journal 2024;45(27):2439-2452
corrections.name: xylitol
corrections.description_en: A polyol sweetener used in sugar-free gum, sweets and drinks. It is dose-dependently laxative, and a 2024 European Heart Journal study linked circulating xylitol to major cardiovascular events and showed heightened platelet reactivity in every volunteer after ingestion. The evidence is associative plus mechanistic rather than causal, but it places xylitol alongside erythritol rather than with the other polyols.

corrections._reason: Merges the duplicate pair 'gelatine' / 'gelatine e441'.
corrections.name: gelatine
corrections.description_en: Collagen extracted from animal skin and bone by acid or alkali treatment (E441). It is a safe, protein-based gelling agent, though of animal origin and low in nutritional value. Not suitable for vegetarians, or for halal and kosher diets unless certified.

corrections._reason: Exact duplicate of 'gelatine', to be removed after the aliases are merged.
corrections.name: gelatine e441

corrections._reason: The database had E217 (the sodium salt) but not E216, which is the form most often seen on labels.
corrections._source: Removed from the EU list in 2006 following EFSA 2004 opinion (Oishi 2002 study) ; banned in California foods in 2023
corrections.name: propyl paraben
corrections.description_en: A paraben preservative removed from the EU list of authorised food additives in 2006, after EFSA judged that the presumed safe intake was no longer valid because of effects on sex hormones and male reproductive organs in young rats. No food ADI has been accepted since. It is still permitted in US food, and was banned from foods in California in 2023.

corrections._reason: E306 is the most common natural antioxidant on labels, missing while E307/E308/E309 were present.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2015;13(9):4247
corrections.name: extrait riche en tocopherols
corrections.description_en: A natural vitamin E mixture extracted from vegetable oils (E306), used to stop fats going rancid. EFSA's 2015 re-evaluation of the tocopherol family found no safety concern at dietary exposures. It is one of the most benign antioxidants available, and a better sign on a label than synthetic BHA or BHT.

corrections._reason: Liver is so concentrated in preformed vitamin A that health agencies advise avoiding it entirely during pregnancy. The entry did not say so.
corrections._source: NHS ; Sante publique France ; EFSA tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A
corrections.name: foie
corrections.description_en: Exceptionally rich in vitamin A, B12, iron and copper - one of the most nutrient-dense foods there is. Its preformed vitamin A is so concentrated that health agencies advise pregnant women to avoid liver and liver products entirely, and a single weekly portion is enough for everyone else.

corrections._reason: 'raw milk' was an alias of 'lait de chevre' and inherited its green badge. It is advised against for pregnant women, young children, older adults and immunocompromised people.
corrections._source: Health Canada / MAPAQ (sale prohibited in Canada) ; ANSES ; CDC
corrections.name: lait cru
corrections.description_en: Milk that has not been pasteurised. It keeps enzymes and flavour that heat destroys, but it can carry listeria, salmonella and E. coli, which is why health agencies advise against it for pregnant women, young children, older adults and anyone immunocompromised. Its sale for direct consumption is prohibited in Canada.

corrections._reason: Alias 'lait cru' removed - moved to its own entry.
corrections.name: lait de chevre
corrections.description_en: Smaller fat globules in goat, sheep and buffalo milk may make them easier to digest for some people. Nutritionally they are close to cow's milk, with slightly more medium-chain fats.

corrections._reason: One to two nuts cover the daily selenium requirement; a regular handful exceeds the tolerable upper intake (selenosis).
corrections._source: EFSA tolerable upper intake level for selenium (revised 2023) ; USDA FoodData Central
corrections.name: noix du bresil
corrections.description_en: The richest natural source of selenium on the planet, which supports thyroid function and antioxidant defences. One or two nuts already cover a full day's requirement, and eating them by the handful every day can exceed the tolerable upper intake - a rare case where a whole food needs a portion limit.

corrections._reason: Green badge untenable for a concentrated extract: the EU requires warning labelling above 800 mg EGCG per day for liver injury. The infusion remains fine, hence Occasional rather than harsher.
corrections._source: EFSA opinion of 14 March 2018 ; Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/2340
corrections.name: egcg
corrections.description_en: The main catechin in green tea, a well-studied antioxidant. Drunk as an infusion it raises no concern. As a concentrated extract it is a different matter: EFSA found in 2018 that 800 mg of EGCG per day or more from supplements raises liver enzymes, and the EU now requires warning labelling on green tea extracts. Read it as a good sign in tea, a caution in a supplement.

corrections._reason: Kombu is the most iodine-dense food known and can disturb thyroid function. The database already flags hijiki arsenic; the same logic was expected here.
corrections._source: ANSES opinion on seaweed consumption and iodine intake ; UK Food Standards Agency
corrections.name: algue
corrections.description_en: Seaweed provides iodine, iron, magnesium and soluble fibre, supporting thyroid function and overall nutrition. Nori and wakame are moderate, but kombu is by far the most iodine-dense food known and can disturb thyroid function if eaten regularly - health agencies advise limiting it, and using it for stock rather than eating it.

corrections._reason: Text bug: the description was copied from 'lecithine de soja' and talked about soy and GM crops on a sunflower entry.
corrections.name: lecithine de tournesol
corrections.description_en: A natural emulsifier pressed from sunflower seeds, used to blend fat and water. Unlike soy lecithin it is obtained mechanically rather than with solvents, involves no GM crop and carries no soy allergen - which makes it the cleanest emulsifier commonly found on a label.

corrections._reason: Food-grade citric acid is not extracted from citrus; it is produced by fermenting sugar with Aspergillus niger. It also contradicted the E331 entry, which correctly says there is no natural food form.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 231/2012, E330 specifications ; EFSA Journal 2014;12(11):3898
corrections.name: acide citrique
corrections.description_en: The acid that gives citrus fruit its sharpness - though the E330 on a label is produced industrially by fermenting sugar with Aspergillus niger, not extracted from lemons. It is one of the most benign additives there is, used to adjust acidity and protect colour. Its only real drawback is that it erodes tooth enamel in acidic drinks.

corrections._reason: Curcumin's anti-inflammatory effects are documented at supplement doses, not at the trace dose of a colouring, where bioavailability is negligible.
corrections._source: EFSA Journal 2010;8(9):1679 (E100 re-evaluation) ; curcumin bioavailability literature
corrections.name: curcumine
corrections.description_en: The yellow pigment of turmeric (E100), used as a natural colouring. It is a plant-derived alternative to synthetic yellow dyes and raises no safety concern at food levels. The anti-inflammatory effects attributed to curcumin come from concentrated supplement doses, not from the trace amount used to colour a food.

corrections._reason: Celery powder is the nitrate vehicle used in charcuterie labelled 'no nitrites added'. The database badged nitrites red and their natural source green.
corrections._source: USDA/FDA labelling rules for 'uncured' meats ; celery-curing literature (identical nitroso-compounds formed)
corrections.name: poudre de celeri
corrections.description_en: Celery stalk or celeriac, simply dried and ground - harmless as a seasoning. Worth knowing, though, that the meat industry uses celery powder and celery juice as a natural nitrate source to cure meat labelled "no nitrites added": the body converts that nitrate to nitrite and the same nitroso-compounds form. On a charcuterie label it is a curing agent, not a vegetable.

corrections._reason: Three distinct substances merged under one keyword set (allulose, tagatose, chicory inulin). Allulose is also not authorised in the EU, making a green badge misleading for the France market.
corrections._source: Regulation (EU) 2015/2283 (novel food) ; EFSA opinion adopted 6 May 2025, authorisation not granted to date
corrections.name: allulose
corrections.description_en: A rare sugar that sweetens with almost no calories and no effect on blood glucose. It is authorised in the United States, Canada, Japan and Korea, but not in the European Union or the UK, where it is still going through novel food assessment. Large amounts cause bloating and digestive upset.

corrections._reason: An unqualified green badge is misleading in France: only an aqueous decoction is authorised in the EU, not purified mogroside V, which is the form in most North American products.
corrections._source: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2345 ; food additive application under EFSA assessment (EFSA-Q-2025-00007)
corrections.name: fruit du moine
corrections.description_en: A sweetener from the luo han guo fruit, with no calories and no effect on blood sugar. It has a long history of use in Asia and is widely permitted in North America. In the EU only an aqueous decoction of the fruit has been authorised, while purified mogroside V - the form used in most imported products - is still awaiting authorisation.

corrections._reason: The description described wholemeal but the aliases captured 'farine de ble' and 'wheat flour', i.e. refined white flour - badged green while white bread was yellow.
corrections.name: ble
corrections.description_en: Whole wheat - the intact grain with its bran and germ - supplies fibre, B vitamins, magnesium and plant protein. Refining strips most of that away, so the wholemeal version is a different food nutritionally from white flour.

corrections._reason: Recovers the aliases stripped from 'ble'. White flour cannot be green when the white bread it produces is yellow.
corrections.name: farine de ble blanche
corrections.description_en: Wheat flour with the bran and germ milled out. It keeps the starch and part of the protein but loses most of the fibre, magnesium and B vitamins of the grain, and raises blood sugar faster. Wholemeal flour is the same ingredient with its nutrition intact.

corrections._reason: Same issue as wheat: brown rice description, aliases capturing generic white rice. 'farine de riz' was already Occasional.
corrections.name: riz
corrections.description_en: Brown rice keeps its bran and germ, and with them fibre, B vitamins, magnesium and manganese that support digestion and energy production. White rice is the same grain with those layers polished off, which removes most of the nutrients and raises the glycemic response.

corrections._reason: Recovers the generic aliases stripped from 'riz'.
corrections.name: riz blanc
corrections.description_en: Rice polished to remove the bran and germ. It is easy to digest and keeps well, but the milling takes away most of the fibre, magnesium and B vitamins and leaves a starch with a high glycemic response. Basmati has a lower glycemic index than short-grain white rice.

corrections._reason: Corn starch, potato starch, wheat starch and generic starch are all Occasional. Tapioca starch is the same refined carbohydrate and was alone in Approved.
corrections.name: fecule de tapioca
corrections.description_en: Starch extracted from the cassava root. It is naturally gluten-free and useful as a thickener, but like every isolated starch it is a refined carbohydrate with a high glycemic response and none of the fibre or minerals of the root.

corrections._reason: Agave syrup is Occasional for its fructose load, but honey was Approved 'no risk' at 80% sugar. A green badge on a sugar undermines the whole badge system.
corrections._source: WHO free sugars guideline (honey is explicitly counted as a free sugar)
corrections.name: miel
corrections.description_en: Raw honey brings antioxidants, enzymes and antibacterial compounds that refined sugar does not have. It is still around 80% sugar, and the WHO counts it as a free sugar exactly like table sugar - a better sweetener, not a free one. Never give honey to a baby under one year old, because of the risk of infant botulism.

corrections._reason: Same logic as honey; consistency with agave syrup already in Occasional.
corrections._source: WHO free sugars guideline
corrections.name: sirop d'erable
corrections.description_en: Maple syrup is simply concentrated maple sap, and it carries manganese, zinc and polyphenols that refining would remove. It is nonetheless about two thirds sugar and counts as a free sugar in dietary guidelines - a whole-food sweetener to use sparingly.

corrections._reason: Same logic: coconut sugar, date sugar and whole cane sugar were Approved 'no risk'.
corrections._source: WHO free sugars guideline
corrections.name: sucre de canne complet
corrections.description_en: Unrefined cane sugar (rapadura, panela, muscovado, jaggery) keeps the molasses and with it iron, potassium and polyphenols that white sugar has lost. It is nonetheless still 85 to 95% sucrose and behaves in the body much like table sugar. Better, not harmless.

corrections._reason: 'jus concentre' is Occasional and 'concentre de fruits' is Processed, but pressed juice was Approved. Without fibre, juice sugar behaves as a free sugar.
corrections._source: WHO free sugars definition (explicitly includes fruit juice)
corrections.name: jus de fruits frais
corrections.description_en: Freshly pressed juice keeps the vitamins and polyphenols of the fruit, but pressing removes the fibre that slows sugar absorption. The WHO counts fruit juice as a free sugar for that reason, and a glass concentrates the sugar of several pieces of fruit. Whole fruit is always the better version; vegetable-based juices avoid most of the issue.

corrections._reason: Polydextrose is Occasional for bloating; inulin was Approved although it is far more fermentable and a major FODMAP.
corrections.name: inuline
corrections.description_en: A prebiotic fibre from chicory root or agave that feeds beneficial gut bacteria. It is genuinely useful, but it is also one of the most fermentable fibres there is: added to industrial products to boost the fibre figure on the label, it commonly causes bloating and gas, and it is poorly tolerated in irritable bowel syndrome.

corrections._reason: The generic aliases 'saumon' and 'salmon' routed all salmon to the green badge, neutralising the 'saumon d'elevage' entry even though most salmon sold is farmed.
corrections.name: saumon sauvage
corrections.description_en: Wild salmon provides omega-3 EPA and DHA for brain and heart function, along with vitamin D and astaxanthin. It is leaner than farmed salmon and free of the feed, treatments and added colourants of aquaculture.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: mustard + soy sauce + fish sauce + hoisin + oyster sauce + miso + natto + tempeh under one 'rich in probiotics' description. False for mustard and for all pasteurised sauces, and it hid a very high sodium content.
corrections.name: moutarde
corrections.description_en: Mustard is simply crushed mustard seed with vinegar and salt. It adds flavour for almost no calories and keeps the antioxidant compounds of the seed. Dijon and wholegrain versions contain little beyond seed, vinegar, water and salt.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'moutarde'. Korea market: sodium is the real issue, and cheap soy sauce is acid-hydrolysed (3-MCPD) rather than brewed.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 - maximum levels for 3-MCPD in hydrolysed vegetable protein and soy sauce
corrections.name: sauce soja
corrections.description_en: Traditionally brewed soy sauce is fermented for months and carries the depth that comes with it. Two things are worth checking on the label: it is extremely salty, so a few tablespoons cover a large share of the daily sodium limit; and cheaper versions are made by acid hydrolysis rather than brewing, a process that can generate 3-MCPD, which the EU caps by law.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'moutarde'. Miso, natto and tempeh are genuine live ferments and deserve green, unlike the sauces.
corrections.name: miso
corrections.description_en: Soybeans fermented with koji over months, eaten as a paste. Unpasteurised miso, natto and tempeh carry live cultures and enzymes that support digestion, along with complete plant protein. Miso is salty enough to count as a seasoning rather than an ingredient.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'moutarde'. Hoisin is mostly sugar; oyster sauce routinely contains modified starch, caramel colour and flavour enhancers.
corrections.name: sauce hoisin
corrections.description_en: A sweet, thick condiment built mainly on sugar and fermented soybean paste, usually alongside modified starch, caramel colour and flavour enhancers. Oyster sauce is formulated the same way. They are industrial sauces rather than traditional ferments - heavy in both sugar and sodium.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'moutarde'. Fish sauce is a genuine traditional ferment but extremely salty.
corrections.name: sauce poisson
corrections.description_en: Anchovies salted and fermented for months, the backbone of South-East Asian cooking. It is a genuine traditional ferment rich in free amino acids, and it is also one of the saltiest condiments in any kitchen - a teaspoon carries as much sodium as a portion of crisps.

corrections._reason: IMPORTANT IARC UPDATE: talc moved from Group 2B to Group 2A in July 2024 (Monographs vol. 136, published 2025). The entry still reflected the old classification.
corrections._source: IARC Monographs vol. 136 (2024-2025) ; The Lancet Oncology 2024;25(8):962-963
corrections.name: talc alimentaire
corrections.description_en: Food-grade talc (E553b) used to stop powders sticking and clumping. IARC reclassified talc as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans, in 2024, on limited evidence in humans, sufficient evidence in animals and strong mechanistic evidence. A separate and older concern is contamination with asbestos, which occurs naturally alongside talc deposits and is a confirmed Group 1 carcinogen.

corrections._reason: Several food agencies advise AVOIDING hijiki outright because of inorganic arsenic, an IARC Group 1 carcinogen. An orange badge was weaker than the authorities' own message.
corrections._source: UK Food Standards Agency ; Health Canada ; Food Safety Authority of Ireland - advice not to eat hijiki
corrections.name: hijiki
corrections.description_en: A brown seaweed that accumulates inorganic arsenic, an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen, at levels far above any other edible seaweed. The food agencies of the UK, Canada and Ireland do not merely advise moderation: they advise not eating it at all, and choosing another seaweed instead.

corrections._reason: Azodicarbonamide and potassium bromate, both EU-banned, are Ultra toxic. E171, EU-banned in 2022 because genotoxicity could NOT be ruled out, was only Processed - a heavier ground for a lighter badge.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63 ; EFSA Journal 2021;19(5):6585
corrections.name: dioxyde de titane
corrections.description_en: A white colouring (E171) used in sweets, sauces and supplements. The EU banned it as a food additive in August 2022 after EFSA concluded that a concern for genotoxicity could not be ruled out and that no safe daily intake could be set. It remains permitted in the United States and in cosmetics.

corrections._reason: CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER DRAFT. The original entry rested on a vague heavy-metal contamination claim. I had replaced it with a claim that E542 is no longer authorised in the EU - but sources conflict on that point (E542 still has specifications in Regulation 231/2012, while several additive databases list it as not in the Union list). Rather than assert a regulatory status I cannot verify against the primary text, this version states only what is certain.
corrections._source: Commission Regulation (EU) 231/2012 (E542 specifications exist) ; EU Annex II status could not be confirmed - claim deliberately omitted
corrections.name: phosphate d'os
corrections.description_en: Bone phosphate (E542), a calcium phosphate obtained by degreasing and calcining animal bones, used in small amounts to keep powders free-flowing. It is of animal origin, so it does not suit vegetarian, vegan, halal or kosher diets unless specifically certified, and it adds to total phosphate intake, which EFSA already considers high in European diets. Its use in food today is marginal.

corrections._reason: Spirulina is widely promoted as a B12 source. Its B12 is a biologically inactive pseudo-vitamin in humans. Important for a vegetarian audience.
corrections._source: Watanabe et al., pseudo-cobalamin in cyanobacteria ; Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics position on vegetarian diets
corrections.name: spiruline
corrections.description_en: A cyanobacterium dried into powder, dense in plant protein, iron and antioxidants. One caveat matters: the B12 it contains is pseudo-B12, inactive in humans, so it cannot be counted as a B12 source on a plant-based diet. Sourcing also matters, since poorly controlled production can carry microcystin contamination.

corrections._reason: Royal jelly and propolis are documented causes of severe allergic reaction, including anaphylaxis, and are contraindicated in asthma. A green 'no risk' badge was untenable. Claim calibrated: severe reactions are rare but well documented.
corrections._source: Published anaphylaxis case reports for royal jelly ; Australian and European agency advisories
corrections.name: gelee royale
corrections.description_en: Bee products carrying enzymes, amino acids and antibacterial compounds. They are also documented allergens: royal jelly and propolis have caused severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, rare but well recorded, and are best avoided by people with asthma or a known allergy to bee products. Pollen can trigger reactions in people allergic to the source plants.

corrections._reason: 'klamath' (Aphanizomenon flos-aquae) was an alias of chlorella although it is a different species with a different risk profile.
corrections._source: ANSES opinion on cyanobacteria supplements
corrections.name: chlorella
corrections.description_en: A freshwater microalga dried into powder or tablets, rich in protein, iron and chlorophyll. Because it absorbs what its growing water contains, the quality of sourcing decides whether it also carries heavy metals - certified production matters more here than for most foods.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'chlorella' - different species, different risk.
corrections._source: ANSES ; literature on microcystins in Aphanizomenon flos-aquae
corrections.name: klamath
corrections.description_en: A wild-harvested cyanobacterium (Aphanizomenon flos-aquae) sold as a supplement. Because it is gathered from an open lake rather than cultivated, batches can be contaminated with microcystins, liver toxins produced by other cyanobacteria growing alongside it. Health agencies have repeatedly flagged this, and it is not recommended for children or during pregnancy.

corrections._reason: Taro and yam were aliases of potato although they are TOXIC RAW. The solanine issue in green or sprouted potatoes was also missing.
corrections._source: EFSA 2020 opinion on glycoalkaloids in potatoes ; literature on calcium oxalate in taro
corrections.name: pomme de terre
corrections.description_en: Rich in potassium, vitamin C and fibre when the skin is kept on - a genuinely nutritious whole vegetable. Two things to know: potatoes that have turned green or sprouted accumulate solanine, which is bitter and toxic, so those parts should be cut away generously; and frying or roasting at high heat is what generates acrylamide.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'pomme de terre': these roots are toxic raw, which the potato entry could not carry.
corrections.name: taro
corrections.description_en: Starchy tropical roots that must always be cooked. Raw taro and raw yam contain calcium oxalate crystals and other compounds that irritate the mouth and digestive tract; cooking destroys them. Once cooked they are a good source of complex carbohydrate, potassium and fibre.

corrections._reason: 'bamboo shoots' was an alias of okra. Fresh bamboo shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides and must be boiled before eating.
corrections._source: EFSA / FAO literature on taxiphyllin in bamboo shoots
corrections.name: okra
corrections.description_en: Okra provides soluble fibre that helps regulate blood sugar and cholesterol, with very few calories. Its mucilage is what thickens stews and gumbo.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'okra'.
corrections.name: pousses de bambou
corrections.description_en: Bamboo shoots are low in calories and a good source of fibre and potassium, but fresh shoots contain cyanogenic glycosides and must be boiled before eating - canned shoots are already processed and safe. Bean sprouts and lotus root, often sold alongside them, raise no such issue.

corrections._reason: Soft ripened cheeses are subject to a formal pregnancy avoidance recommendation (listeria). Same class of omission as liver and raw milk.
corrections._source: Health Canada ; ANSES ; NHS pregnancy advice
corrections.name: brie
corrections.description_en: Soft ripened cheeses provide calcium, protein and vitamin B12, and develop their character through surface moulds. Because their moisture and low acidity suit listeria, health agencies advise pregnant women to avoid soft ripened cheeses unless they are made from pasteurised milk or have been cooked until steaming hot.

corrections._reason: Same pregnancy recommendation for blue cheeses, plus a very high sodium content that was missing.
corrections._source: Health Canada ; ANSES ; NHS pregnancy advice
corrections.name: roquefort
corrections.description_en: Blue cheeses concentrate calcium, protein and B12, and their moulds give them their character. They are among the saltiest cheeses there are, and health agencies advise pregnant women to avoid blue-veined cheese unless it has been cooked until steaming hot.

corrections._reason: The description mentioned seaweed, which is not even in the aliases, and omitted that crustaceans and molluscs are a mandatory declarable allergen, plus the raw oyster risk.
corrections._source: Regulation (EU) 1169/2011, Annex II (allergens) ; Health Canada advice on raw molluscs
corrections.name: crevette
corrections.description_en: Shellfish supply high-quality protein, zinc, selenium, iodine and vitamin B12 for very little fat. Two practical points: crustaceans and molluscs are among the allergens the EU requires to be declared, and reactions to them are often severe; and raw oysters and clams carry a norovirus and vibrio risk, which is why they are not advised during pregnancy.

corrections._reason: Halibut and sturgeon were aliases of the lean low-mercury white fish entry. Halibut is on the FDA/EPA 'Good Choices' list (1 serving per week), not the 'Best Choices' list.
corrections._source: FDA/EPA Advice About Eating Fish (2021 update) - Best Choices vs Good Choices categories
corrections.name: cabillaud
corrections.description_en: Lean white fish provide complete protein, iodine, selenium and B12 with very little fat, and sit among the lowest-mercury species there are - which is why the FDA and EPA place them on the Best Choices list, two to three servings a week.

corrections._reason: CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER DRAFT. I had grouped halibut with swordfish and shark. Verification shows they are in two different FDA/EPA categories: halibut is 'Good Choices' (1 serving a week), swordfish and shark are 'Choices to Avoid'. They now have separate entries.
corrections._source: FDA/EPA Advice About Eating Fish - Good Choices category
corrections.name: fletan
corrections.description_en: A large flatfish with firm white flesh and a good omega-3 content. Being a big predator it accumulates more methylmercury than small white fish, which puts it on the FDA and EPA Good Choices list: one serving a week rather than the two to three allowed for lean white fish. Sturgeon falls in the same group.

corrections._reason: These species are on the FDA/EPA 'Choices to Avoid' list and were absent from the database entirely.
corrections._source: FDA/EPA Advice About Eating Fish - Choices to Avoid category (mercury above 0.46 ppm)
corrections.name: espadon
corrections.description_en: Long-lived top predators that concentrate the most methylmercury of any commercial fish. The FDA and EPA place swordfish, shark, marlin, king mackerel, bigeye tuna, orange roughy and Gulf tilefish on the Choices to Avoid list: pregnant women, breastfeeding women and children should not eat them at all, and other adults only rarely.

corrections._reason: Caviar is one of the saltiest foods there is (often over 1.5 g sodium per 100 g), which was not mentioned although the 'sel' entry is yellow.
corrections.name: caviar
corrections.description_en: Fish roe is rich in omega-3 EPA and DHA, vitamin B12 and vitamin D. It is also salted heavily to preserve it, which makes it one of the saltiest foods on a table - it works as a delicacy in small spoonfuls, not as a portion.

corrections._reason: Korea market: kimchi deserves green, but its salt content matters and diets high in salted foods are an established stomach cancer risk factor, which is particularly relevant in Korea.
corrections._source: World Cancer Research Fund / AICR - Diet, Nutrition, Physical Activity and Stomach Cancer
corrections.name: kimchi
corrections.description_en: Lacto-fermented vegetables rich in live lactic bacteria, fibre, vitamin C and beta-carotene - one of the best-studied traditional ferments there is. Its one drawback is salt: kimchi is brined, and diets very high in salted foods are an established risk factor for stomach cancer, so it works best as a side dish rather than a main portion.

corrections._reason: Korea market: jeotgal is seafood preserved in salt, with an extreme sodium content. A green 'no risk' badge was not defensible.
corrections._source: World Cancer Research Fund / AICR
corrections.name: jeotgal
corrections.description_en: Seafood salted and fermented for months, used as a seasoning and as a base for kimchi. It is a genuine traditional ferment, and it is also preserved in enough salt to make it one of the highest-sodium foods in any cuisine - a condiment by the spoonful, never a portion.

corrections._reason: The description itself noted that industrial versions contain glucose-fructose syrup, while the badge stayed green 'no risk'.
corrections.name: gochujang
corrections.description_en: A Korean fermented paste of chilli, glutinous rice and soybeans. The traditional version is a genuine ferment; most supermarket jars list glucose-fructose syrup among the main ingredients, which puts them closer to a sweet sauce than to a ferment. The ingredient list decides which one you have.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: hummus merged with guacamole, tzatziki, aioli, salsa verde and romesco. Aioli is essentially oil and egg, unrelated to chickpeas.
corrections.name: humus maison
corrections.description_en: Cooked chickpeas blended with tahini, olive oil, lemon and garlic - plant protein, fibre, unsaturated fat and calcium in one spread. Homemade versions contain nothing else; industrial tubs often add preservatives and cheaper oils.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'humus maison' - vegetable and yoghurt based dips, different composition.
corrections.name: tzatziki
corrections.description_en: Dips built on vegetables, yoghurt or nuts: tzatziki from cucumber and yoghurt, guacamole from avocado, baba ganoush from grilled aubergine, romesco and salsa verde from peppers, nuts and herbs. Made at home they are whole ingredients blended together, with nothing added.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'humus maison': aioli is an oil-and-egg emulsion, nutritionally unrelated to a vegetable dip.
corrections.name: aioli
corrections.description_en: An emulsion of oil, egg yolk and garlic - essentially a garlic mayonnaise. Made with olive oil it is a good fat, but it is almost entirely fat: a couple of tablespoons carry more calories than the dish they accompany.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: kaffir lime leaf merged with wasabi, horseradish, lemongrass, galangal, fresh turmeric and curry leaf - botanically and nutritionally unrelated.
corrections.name: feuille de kaffir
corrections.description_en: Aromatic leaves and rhizomes used fresh in South-East Asian cooking - kaffir lime leaf, lemongrass, galangal, fresh turmeric, ginger root and curry leaf. They are whole plant parts, used in small amounts, and carry the essential oils and antioxidants of the fresh plant.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'feuille de kaffir'. Tube wasabi is almost always dyed horseradish - useful information for the user.
corrections.name: wasabi
corrections.description_en: Wasabi and horseradish are pungent roots from the brassica family, grated fresh and used in tiny amounts. Worth knowing that most wasabi sold in tubes and served in restaurants outside Japan is horseradish coloured green, with mustard and dye rather than real wasabi rhizome - the ingredient list will say.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: sourdough merged with naan, chapati, roti, injera, lavash, pita and tortilla - breads, usually made with refined flour, badged green by inheritance.
corrections.name: levain
corrections.description_en: A natural starter of wild yeasts and lactic bacteria. Long sourdough fermentation breaks down part of the gluten and the phytates that block mineral absorption, which makes sourdough bread more digestible and its magnesium, zinc and iron more available than in yeasted bread.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'levain'. These flatbreads are mostly refined flour - consistency with 'pain blanc', already Occasional.
corrections.name: pain plat
corrections.description_en: Flatbreads such as pita, naan, chapati, roti, lavash and tortilla. Made with wholemeal flour they are a good bread; made with refined white flour, which is the usual case, they behave like white bread, and industrial versions add oils, sugar and preservatives on top.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: lacto-fermented vegetables merged with kombucha and kvass, which are fermented drinks and often heavily sweetened.
corrections.name: cornichon naturel
corrections.description_en: Vegetables preserved by lacto-fermentation in brine rather than vinegar. Live bacteria and organic acids survive in the jar as long as it has not been pasteurised, which supports gut flora. The salt in the brine is the only thing to keep an eye on.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'cornichon naturel': commercial kombucha commonly carries 20 to 40 g of sugar per bottle.
corrections.name: kombucha
corrections.description_en: Sweetened tea fermented by a culture of bacteria and yeast. The fermentation consumes part of the sugar and produces organic acids and live cultures, but commercial bottles are usually sweetened again afterwards and can carry as much sugar as a soft drink. The nutrition label settles it, not the health framing.

corrections._reason: 'date syrup' was an alias of yacon syrup although it is an ordinary concentrated sugar without the fructo-oligosaccharides of yacon.
corrections.name: sirop de yacon
corrections.description_en: Syrup from the yacon root, unusual in that most of its sweetness comes from fructo-oligosaccharides that the body does not absorb, so it feeds gut bacteria instead of raising blood sugar. Large amounts cause bloating for the same reason.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'sirop de yacon' - consistency with the treatment of other natural sugars.
corrections._source: WHO free sugars guideline
corrections.name: sirop de dattes
corrections.description_en: Dates cooked down into a syrup. It keeps some of the potassium and polyphenols of the fruit, but the fibre is largely gone and what remains is concentrated fruit sugar, counted as a free sugar in dietary guidelines.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: melon and watermelon were receiving a description about pomegranate and kiwi. No botanical or nutritional relation.
corrections.name: grenade
corrections.description_en: Pomegranate seeds are dense in punicalagins and anthocyanins, among the most concentrated antioxidants in any fruit, along with fibre and vitamin K.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'grenade'.
corrections.name: melon
corrections.description_en: Melons and watermelon are more than 90% water, which makes them low in calories while supplying potassium, vitamin C and, in the orange and red varieties, beta-carotene and lycopene. Their sugar is diluted enough that a generous portion stays modest.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'grenade'.
corrections.name: kiwi
corrections.description_en: One of the richest fruits in vitamin C, alongside fibre, potassium and actinidin, an enzyme that helps break down protein and eases digestion.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry (quince, mirabelle, greengage and morello cherry are unrelated to rhubarb) plus a real omission: rhubarb LEAVES are toxic, only the stalk is edible.
corrections._source: Toxicological literature on oxalic acid in rhubarb leaves
corrections.name: rhubarbe
corrections.description_en: Rhubarb stalks are very low in sugar and high in fibre and vitamin K, which makes them one of the few fruits used in desserts that adds almost no sweetness of its own. Only the stalk is edible: the leaves contain enough oxalic acid to be genuinely toxic and must never be eaten.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'rhubarbe': stone and pome fruits, unrelated.
corrections.name: coing
corrections.description_en: Quince, mirabelle, greengage and morello cherry are stone or pome fruits eaten cooked or fresh, supplying fibre, potassium and polyphenols. Quince is always cooked, being too astringent raw.

corrections._reason: Catch-all entry: tamarind, tamarillo, physalis and feijoa were receiving a description about the resistant starch of plantain.
corrections.name: plantain
corrections.description_en: Plantain is a starchy banana always eaten cooked. Green plantain is high in resistant starch, which feeds gut bacteria and blunts the glycemic response; as it ripens that starch turns to sugar.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'plantain'.
corrections.name: tamarin
corrections.description_en: Tamarind pulp is tangy and high in fibre, magnesium and polyphenols, used as a souring agent across South Asian and Latin American cooking. It is also naturally sugar-dense, so the concentrated pastes and blocks count as a sweet-sour ingredient rather than a fruit portion.

corrections._reason: Split out of 'plantain'.
corrections.name: physalis
corrections.description_en: Small tart fruits eaten fresh - physalis, tamarillo and feijoa. They are low in sugar and supply vitamin C, fibre and carotenoids.

corrections._reason: The generic 'boisson vegetale' alias was badged green although most commercial references contain added sugar, oils and gums. The description already said 'best chosen without added sugars' without the badge reflecting it.
corrections.name: lait d'amande
corrections.description_en: Plant drinks are a good dairy alternative when the ingredient list is short: water, the nut or grain, and nothing else. Most supermarket versions add sugar, oils, gums and emulsifiers, and many contain only 2 to 3% almond, which leaves a drink with almost no protein. Choose unsweetened and fortified with calcium.

corrections._reason: Ginseng interacts with anticoagulants and diabetes medication and is not recommended in pregnancy. A green 'no risk' badge for a concentrated extract was not defensible.
corrections._source: EMA monograph on Panax ginseng ; warfarin interaction literature
corrections.name: ginseng
corrections.description_en: An Asian root traditionally used against fatigue, sold today mostly as a concentrated extract. It is not inert: it interacts with anticoagulants and diabetes medication, can disturb sleep at higher doses, and is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding.

corrections._reason: CALIBRATED AFTER VERIFICATION. Reishi liver injury is real but rare: the NIH LiverTox database calls clinically apparent injury 'extremely rare', and reported cases mostly involve the powdered form, concurrent alcohol or pre-existing liver disease. My earlier draft overstated it; this version states the frequency honestly. Occasional badge kept for consistency with ashwagandha.
corrections._source: NIH LiverTox ; Yuen et al., J Hepatol 2004;41:686-7 ; Wanmuang et al., J Med Assoc Thai 2007;90:179-81 ; Cochrane review on Ganoderma lucidum
corrections.name: reishi
corrections.description_en: Medicinal mushrooms sold as dried powder or concentrated extract. They supply beta-glucans and are well tolerated as a food. As a supplement, reishi has been associated with rare cases of liver injury - the NIH LiverTox database describes clinically apparent injury as extremely rare, and reported cases mostly involve the unextracted powdered form, alcohol use or existing liver disease. It can also interact with anticoagulants. Treat it as a supplement with its own precautions, not as an ordinary mushroom.
